context: Select and write the correct answers for the following multiple choice type of questions :
stem: Which of the following is NOT an elastomer?
solution:
**(D)** polyethene

An **elastomer** is a polymer whose chains are held together by only weak, widely spaced cross links. The chains are coiled at rest, straighten when the material is stretched and recoil when the stress is removed, which is what gives rubber-like elasticity.

Vulcanized rubber, buna-S and neoprene are all elastomers: each is built from a diene monomer, so the chains keep the residual double bonds and the irregular, coiled shape that elasticity needs.

Polyethene is made by addition polymerisation of ethene into long, unbranched, closely packed chains. These pack into a partly crystalline solid held by strong intermolecular forces, so it softens on heating and hardens on cooling instead of stretching and recoiling.

\(\therefore\) polyethene is a **thermoplastic**, not an elastomer.

context: Select and write the correct answers for the following multiple choice type of questions :
stem: Anisole reacts with HI at 398K to form \(-\)
solution:
**(B)** benzenol

Anisole is methoxybenzene, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}O{-}CH_3}\). Hydroiodic acid cleaves the ether linkage, and the question is which of the two \(\mathrm{C{-}O}\) bonds breaks.

The bond to the ring does **not** break. The oxygen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, so the \(\mathrm{O{-}C_{aryl}}\) bond acquires partial double bond character and is both shorter and stronger than an ordinary single bond. The iodide ion therefore attacks the methyl carbon, which is an ordinary \(sp^3\) centre open to nucleophilic substitution.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}O{-}CH_3 + HI \longrightarrow C_6H_5{-}OH + CH_3I}\)

\(\therefore\) the aromatic product is phenol, which is named **benzenol**. Iodobenzene would require the aryl-oxygen bond to break, which is exactly what the resonance prevents.

subtopic: Solubility and Capacity to Dissolve Solute
context: Select and write the correct answers for the following multiple choice type of questions :
stem: Unit of Henry's constant is _____.
solution:
**(A)** \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ bar^{-1}}\)

Henry's law states that the solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the pressure of the gas above the liquid:

\(S = K_H \times P\)

so

\(K_H = \dfrac{S}{P}\)

The unit follows from the units of the two quantities it divides. Solubility \(S\) is a concentration, measured in \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\), and pressure \(P\) is measured in bar.

\(\therefore K_H\) has the unit \(\dfrac{\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}}{\mathrm{bar}} = \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ bar^{-1}}\)

context: Select and write the correct answers for the following multiple choice type of questions :
stem: The shape of bromine penta-fluoride is _____.
solution:
**(D)** Square pyramidal

In \(\mathrm{BrF_5}\) the central bromine atom has 7 valence electrons. Five of them form bonds to the five fluorine atoms, and the remaining two stay as one lone pair.

So bromine carries 5 bond pairs and 1 lone pair, a total of 6 electron pairs. Six pairs arrange themselves octahedrally, which means the hybridisation is \(sp^3d^2\).

Shape is decided by the positions of the ATOMS, not of the electron pairs. Removing one vertex of the octahedron and putting the lone pair there leaves five fluorines: four in a square plane and one above the centre of that square.

\(\therefore\) the molecule is **square pyramidal**. The lone pair also pushes the four basal bonds slightly below the plane, so the \(\mathrm{F{-}Br{-}F}\) angle is a little under \(90^{\circ}\).

context: Select and write the correct answers for the following multiple choice type of questions :
stem: The relation between edge length and radius for body centered cubic structure is \(-\)
solution:
**(B)** \(r = \sqrt{3}\,\dfrac{a}{4}\)

In a body centred cubic cell the particles touch along the **body diagonal**, not along an edge and not along a face diagonal. The corner particle, the central particle and the opposite corner particle lie on one straight line.

For a cube of edge \(a\), the face diagonal is \(\sqrt{2}\,a\) and the body diagonal is

\(\sqrt{a^{2} + (\sqrt{2}a)^{2}} = \sqrt{3}\,a\)

Along that diagonal lie one radius of the first corner particle, the full diameter of the central particle and one radius of the far corner particle:

\(r + 2r + r = 4r = \sqrt{3}\,a\)

\(\therefore r = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}\,a}{4}\)

Option (C) is the face centred cubic relation, where contact is along the face diagonal, and option (A) is the simple cubic one, where contact is along the edge.

context: Select and write the correct answers for the following multiple choice type of questions :
stem: Atomic number of post actinoid element range from\(-\)
solution:
**(D)** 104 – 118

The actinoid series runs from thorium \((Z = 90)\) to lawrencium \((Z = 103)\), the elements in which the \(5f\) orbitals are progressively filled.

The **post actinoid** elements are those that come after the series is complete, so they begin at rutherfordium \((Z = 104)\) and continue to oganesson \((Z = 118)\), the heaviest element so far known. In these elements the \(6d\) orbitals fill, which is why they are placed in the main body of the periodic table rather than in the \(f\)-block rows below it.

\(\therefore\) the range is 104 to 118.

Option (C), 93 to 103, is the set of transuranic actinoids, which are still part of the series and not after it.

context: Select and write the correct answers for the following multiple choice type of questions :
stem: The pH of buffer solution containing 0.05 mol NaF per litre and 0.01 mol HF per litre \((\mathrm{p}K_a = 3.1427)\) is ____.
solution:
**(A)** 3.8417

The solution holds a weak acid, HF, together with its salt, NaF, so it is an **acidic buffer** and the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation applies:

\(\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a + \log\dfrac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}\)

Substituting the given values,

\(\mathrm{pH} = 3.1427 + \log\dfrac{0.05}{0.01}\)

\(\mathrm{pH} = 3.1427 + \log 5\)

\(\mathrm{pH} = 3.1427 + 0.6990\)

\(\therefore \mathrm{pH} = 3.8417\)

The salt is in excess of the acid, so the buffer must be less acidic than \(\mathrm{p}K_a\) alone would give. Option (B) is what you get by forgetting the logarithmic term entirely.

context: Select and write the correct answers for the following multiple choice type of questions :
stem: Preparation of ethanamine from acetonitrile represents \(-\)
solution:
**(B)** Mendius reduction

Acetonitrile is \(\mathrm{CH_3CN}\). Reducing the cyano group with nascent hydrogen, from sodium in alcohol or from \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\), adds four hydrogen atoms across the carbon-nitrogen triple bond:

\(\mathrm{CH_3CN + 4[H] \longrightarrow CH_3CH_2NH_2}\)

The reduction of a nitrile to a primary amine is named the **Mendius reduction**. Note that the carbon count goes up by one relative to the alkyl group that carried the cyanide, which is why this route is useful for ascending a series.

The others do not fit. Gabriel phthalimide synthesis builds a primary amine from an alkyl halide and potassium phthalimide, and cannot make an aromatic amine. Hofmann hypobromite degradation converts an amide to an amine with one carbon LESS. The Sandmeyer reaction replaces a diazonium group by a halide and makes no amine at all.

subtopic: Uses and Environmental Effects of Polyhalogen Compounds
context: Select and write the correct answers for the following multiple choice type of questions :
stem: The source of dichlorocarbene is _____.
solution:
**(C)** chloroform

Dichlorocarbene is \(\mathrm{:CCl_2}\), a neutral carbon carrying two chlorines and one lone pair. It is generated from chloroform, \(\mathrm{CHCl_3}\), by treatment with a strong base such as aqueous KOH.

The base removes the single hydrogen, which is acidic because the three chlorines withdraw electron density:

\(\mathrm{CHCl_3 + KOH \longrightarrow CCl_3^{-} + K^{+} + H_2O}\)

The trichloromethyl anion then loses a chloride ion:

\(\mathrm{CCl_3^{-} \longrightarrow :CCl_2 + Cl^{-}}\)

\(\therefore\) chloroform is the source. This is the species responsible for the Reimer-Tiemann reaction and for the carbylamine test.

Carbon tetrachloride has no hydrogen for the base to remove, and methyl chloride and methylene chloride do not carry enough chlorine to acidify their hydrogens.

context: Select and write the correct answers for the following multiple choice type of questions :
stem: The reagent used to convert acetyl chloride to acetaldehyde is \(-\)
solution:
**(D)** \(\mathrm{H_2/Pd{-}BaSO_4}\)

Converting an acid chloride to an aldehyde is a reduction that must be STOPPED at the aldehyde. Ordinary hydrogenation would carry straight on to the primary alcohol, so the catalyst has to be deliberately weakened.

That is the **Rosenmund reduction**: hydrogen over palladium supported on barium sulfate, with the palladium partially poisoned by sulfur or quinoline.

\(\mathrm{CH_3COCl + H_2 \xrightarrow{Pd/BaSO_4} CH_3CHO + HCl}\)

The barium sulfate support and the poison together lower the activity of the palladium just enough to release the aldehyde before it is reduced further.

The other reagents all reduce something else. \(\mathrm{Zn{\cdot}Hg}\) with concentrated HCl is Clemmensen reduction and takes a carbonyl all the way to \(\mathrm{CH_2}\); hydrazine with KOH is the Wolff-Kishner reduction, which does the same under basic conditions; \(\mathrm{SnCl_2 + HCl}\) is the Stephen reduction, used on a nitrile rather than an acid chloride.

subtopic: Electric Conduction and Conductance of Solutions
stem: Write the relation between conductivity and molar conductivity.
solution:
Molar conductivity is the conducting power of all the ions produced by **one mole** of electrolyte in a solution, so it is obtained by dividing the conductivity by the molar concentration:

\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa}{c}\)

where \(\kappa\) is the conductivity and \(c\) the concentration in \(\mathrm{mol\ m^{-3}}\).

When \(\kappa\) is in \(\mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\) and the concentration is in \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\), a factor of 1000 converts litres to cubic centimetres:

\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{1000\,\kappa}{c}\)

stem: Write the oxidation state of Nickel in \(\mathrm{[Ni(Cl)_4]^{2-}}\) complex ion.
solution:
Let the oxidation state of nickel be \(x\). Each chloride ligand carries a charge of \(-1\), and the sum of all the charges must equal the overall charge on the complex ion:

\(x + 4(-1) = -2\)

\(x - 4 = -2\)

\(\therefore x = +2\)

The oxidation state of nickel is **+2**.

stem: Write the name of nanostructured material used in tyres of car to increase their life.
solution:
**Carbon black** is the nanostructured material used.

It consists of nanoparticles of nearly pure elemental carbon which are blended into the rubber. The particles reinforce the rubber matrix, greatly increasing its tensile strength and resistance to abrasion, so the tread wears down far more slowly and the life of the tyre is increased.

stem: Write the glycosidic linkage present in maltose.
solution:
Maltose is a disaccharide of two glucose units. The linkage joins the anomeric carbon \(\mathrm{C_1}\) of the first glucose to the \(\mathrm{C_4}\) hydroxyl of the second, and the configuration at that anomeric carbon is alpha.

\(\therefore\) maltose contains an **\(\alpha\)-1,4-glycosidic linkage**.

Because only one of the two anomeric carbons is tied up in the linkage, the other is free, which is why maltose is a reducing sugar.

stem: Draw the structure of perchloric acid.
solution:
Perchloric acid is \(\mathrm{HClO_4}\).

The chlorine atom is at the centre, surrounded tetrahedrally by four oxygen atoms. Three of them are joined to chlorine by double bonds, and the fourth carries the acidic hydrogen as an \(\mathrm{O{-}H}\) group:

\(\mathrm{O=Cl(=O)(=O){-}O{-}H}\)

So chlorine is in the \(+7\) oxidation state and is \(sp^3\) hybridised, giving a tetrahedral arrangement about it. The three \(\mathrm{Cl{=}O}\) bonds are equivalent by resonance, which spreads the negative charge of the \(\mathrm{ClO_4^{-}}\) ion over all four oxygens and makes perchloric acid the strongest of the chlorine oxoacids.

stem: Write the trade name of most common thermoplastic polyester.
solution:
The most common thermoplastic polyester is poly(ethylene terephthalate), PET, whose trade name is **Terylene** (also sold as Dacron).

It is made by the condensation polymerisation of ethylene glycol with terephthalic acid, and it is used for synthetic fibre and for beverage bottles.

stem: Calculate change over temperature for a certain reaction, whose \(\Delta H^{\circ}\) is \(-60\) kJ and \(\Delta S^{\circ}\) is \(-150\ \mathrm{JK^{-1}}\).
solution:
The changeover temperature is the temperature at which the reaction stops being spontaneous and becomes non-spontaneous, which is where \(\Delta G^{\circ} = 0\).

\(\Delta G^{\circ} = \Delta H^{\circ} - T\Delta S^{\circ}\)

Setting \(\Delta G^{\circ} = 0\),

\(T = \dfrac{\Delta H^{\circ}}{\Delta S^{\circ}}\)

The two quantities must be in the same energy unit, so convert the enthalpy to joules:

\(\Delta H^{\circ} = -60\ \mathrm{kJ} = -60000\ \mathrm{J}\)

\(T = \dfrac{-60000}{-150}\)

\(\therefore T = 400\ \mathrm{K}\)

Both \(\Delta H^{\circ}\) and \(\Delta S^{\circ}\) are negative, so the reaction is spontaneous below 400 K and non-spontaneous above it.

stem: Write the unit of rate constant of zero order reaction.
solution:
For a zero order reaction the rate does not depend on the concentration of the reactant:

\(\text{rate} = k[A]^{0} = k\)

So the rate constant is numerically equal to the rate itself, and it must carry the units of a rate.

\(\therefore\) the unit of \(k\) is \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\) (equivalently \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ s^{-1}}\)).

stem: Write reactions involved during preparation of Nylon 6, 6 fibre.
solution:
Nylon 6,6 is a **polyamide** made by the condensation polymerisation of two monomers, each of which carries six carbon atoms. That is where the name comes from.

The monomers are hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid:

\(\mathrm{H_2N{-}(CH_2)_6{-}NH_2}\)  (hexamethylenediamine)

\(\mathrm{HOOC{-}(CH_2)_4{-}COOH}\)  (adipic acid)

**Step 1 — salt formation.** Mixing the two in equimolar amounts gives nylon salt, which ensures the exact 1 : 1 ratio the polymer needs:

\(\mathrm{H_2N{-}(CH_2)_6{-}NH_2 + HOOC{-}(CH_2)_4{-}COOH \longrightarrow {}^{-}OOC{-}(CH_2)_4{-}COO^{-}\ {}^{+}H_3N{-}(CH_2)_6{-}NH_3^{+}}\)

**Step 2 — polymerisation.** Heating the salt to about 550 K under pressure drives off water and forms amide linkages:

\(n\,\mathrm{H_2N{-}(CH_2)_6{-}NH_2} + n\,\mathrm{HOOC{-}(CH_2)_4{-}COOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{[{-}NH{-}(CH_2)_6{-}NH{-}CO{-}(CH_2)_4{-}CO{-}]}_n + 2n\,\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The molten polymer is extruded through a spinneret and cold drawn to align the chains, which sets up hydrogen bonds between neighbouring amide groups and gives the fibre its strength.

stem: Derive Ostwald's dilution law equation for a weak acid.
solution:
Consider a weak monobasic acid HA of initial concentration \(c\) which ionises to a degree \(\alpha\):

\(\mathrm{HA \rightleftharpoons H^{+} + A^{-}}\)

Set out the concentrations at equilibrium. Initially only HA is present at concentration \(c\); at equilibrium a fraction \(\alpha\) of it has dissociated:

| | HA | \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) | \(\mathrm{A^{-}}\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| initial | \(c\) | 0 | 0 |
| at equilibrium | \(c(1-\alpha)\) | \(c\alpha\) | \(c\alpha\) |

The dissociation constant is

\(K_a = \dfrac{[\mathrm{H^{+}}][\mathrm{A^{-}}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}\)

Substituting the equilibrium concentrations,

\(K_a = \dfrac{(c\alpha)(c\alpha)}{c(1-\alpha)} = \dfrac{c\alpha^{2}}{1-\alpha}\)

This is **Ostwald's dilution law** in its exact form.

For a weak acid \(\alpha\) is very small, so \(1 - \alpha \approx 1\) and the expression simplifies to

\(K_a = c\alpha^{2}\)

\(\therefore \alpha = \sqrt{\dfrac{K_a}{c}}\)

Since \(c = 1/V\) for dilution volume \(V\), this says \(\alpha \propto \sqrt{V}\): the degree of dissociation of a weak acid increases as the solution is diluted.

stem: Draw the structures of two forms of alanine having \(\mathrm{pH} \le 2\) and \(\mathrm{pH} \ge 10\).
solution:
Alanine is \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH(NH_2){-}COOH}\). It is amphoteric, so which form it takes depends on the pH of the solution.

**At \(\mathrm{pH} \le 2\) — the cationic form.** The solution is strongly acidic, so there is a high concentration of \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\). The carboxylate group is protonated back to \(\mathrm{{-}COOH}\) and the amino group is protonated to \(\mathrm{{-}NH_3^{+}}\):

\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH(NH_3^{+}){-}COOH}\)

The molecule carries a net charge of \(+1\) and migrates towards the cathode in an electric field.

**At \(\mathrm{pH} \ge 10\) — the anionic form.** The solution is strongly basic, so \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) removes the proton from the ammonium group, leaving a free \(\mathrm{{-}NH_2}\), while the carboxyl group stays deprotonated as \(\mathrm{{-}COO^{-}}\):

\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH(NH_2){-}COO^{-}}\)

The molecule carries a net charge of \(-1\) and migrates towards the anode.

Between these two extremes, near the isoelectric point, alanine exists as the **zwitterion** \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH(NH_3^{+}){-}COO^{-}}\), which has no net charge and does not migrate at all.

stem:
Define the following terms :

(a) Intensive property

(b) Standard enthalpy of combustion
solution:
**(a) Intensive property.** A property of a system whose value does not depend on the amount of matter present in the system.

Temperature, pressure, density, refractive index, viscosity and molar volume are intensive. If a sample is divided into two halves, each half has the same value of an intensive property as the whole had. This is what separates them from extensive properties such as mass, volume and enthalpy, which are halved along with the sample.

**(b) Standard enthalpy of combustion.** The enthalpy change when **one mole** of a substance is completely burnt in excess of oxygen, with all the reactants and products in their standard states at a specified temperature, usually 298 K.

It is written \(\Delta_c H^{\circ}\) and is always negative, since combustion is exothermic. The words "one mole" and "completely" are both load-bearing: complete combustion of a hydrocarbon means the carbon must end as \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and not as CO.

stem:
What is the action of following reagents on ethyl amine?

(Indicate by reaction)

(a) Nitrous acid

(b) Chloroform and KOH
solution:
**(a) Nitrous acid.** Ethylamine is a primary aliphatic amine. With nitrous acid, generated in situ from \(\mathrm{NaNO_2}\) and dilute HCl at low temperature, it forms a diazonium salt which is unstable and decomposes at once, giving ethanol and liberating nitrogen gas:

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2 + HNO_2 \longrightarrow C_2H_5OH + N_2\uparrow + H_2O}\)

The brisk effervescence of nitrogen is the test for a primary aliphatic amine. Aromatic diazonium salts, by contrast, are stable enough at 273-278 K to be used in further reactions.

**(b) Chloroform and KOH — the carbylamine reaction.** On warming with chloroform and alcoholic KOH, ethylamine gives ethyl isocyanide, a compound with an extremely offensive smell:

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2 + CHCl_3 + 3KOH \longrightarrow C_2H_5NC + 3KCl + 3H_2O}\)

The reactive species is dichlorocarbene, \(\mathrm{:CCl_2}\), formed from chloroform and the base.

This reaction is given only by **primary** amines, so it serves as a test to distinguish them from secondary and tertiary amines.

subtopic: Electric Conduction and Conductance of Solutions
stem:
(a) State Kohlrausch law of independent migration of ions.

(b) Write Nernst equation to calculate electrode potential.
solution:
**(a) Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions.** At infinite dilution, where the dissociation of an electrolyte is complete and the ions are so far apart that they no longer influence one another, each ion contributes a definite amount to the total molar conductivity that is independent of the other ion it was paired with.

So the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the limiting molar conductivities of its ions:

\(\Lambda_0 = n_{+}\lambda_{0}^{+} + n_{-}\lambda_{0}^{-}\)

where \(n_{+}\) and \(n_{-}\) are the numbers of cations and anions produced by one formula unit.

**(b) Nernst equation for electrode potential.** For the reduction half reaction \(\mathrm{M^{n+} + n e^{-} \longrightarrow M}\),

\(E = E^{\circ} + \dfrac{2.303\,RT}{nF}\log[\mathrm{M^{n+}}]\)

At 298 K, substituting \(R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}mol^{-1}}\) and \(F = 96500\ \mathrm{C\ mol^{-1}}\), the coefficient becomes 0.0592 V:

\(E = E^{\circ} + \dfrac{0.0592}{n}\log[\mathrm{M^{n+}}]\)

subtopic: Position in the Periodic Table and Electronic Configuration
stem:
(a) Write general electronic configuration of 3d series elements.

(b) Write any two points which explain about the colour of a transition metal ion.
solution:
**(a) General electronic configuration.** The 3d series elements follow argon and fill the \(3d\) orbitals while the \(4s\) orbital is already occupied:

\(\mathrm{[Ar]\ 3d^{1-10}\ 4s^{1-2}}\)

Chromium and copper are the exceptions, taking \(3d^{5}4s^{1}\) and \(3d^{10}4s^{1}\) because a half filled and a completely filled \(d\) subshell are extra stable.

**(b) Colour of a transition metal ion.** Two points explain it:

1. **Partly filled \(d\) orbitals.** In a complex the ligands split the five \(d\) orbitals into two sets of different energy. An ion with a partly filled \(d\) subshell can absorb a photon of visible light to promote an electron from the lower set to the higher set. This is a \(d\)-\(d\) transition.

2. **The colour seen is the complement of the colour absorbed.** The energy gap between the two sets corresponds to a particular wavelength in the visible region; that wavelength is removed from white light and the eye perceives what remains.

This is why \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) \((3d^{0})\) and \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) \((3d^{10})\) are colourless: with no partly filled \(d\) subshell, no \(d\)-\(d\) transition is possible.

subtopic: Chemical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones
stem: Explain aldol condensation reaction with respect to ethanal.
solution:
An **aldol condensation** is the reaction of two molecules of an aldehyde or ketone that carries at least one \(\alpha\)-hydrogen, in the presence of dilute alkali, to give a \(\beta\)-hydroxy carbonyl compound. Ethanal has three \(\alpha\)-hydrogens, so it undergoes the reaction readily.

**Step 1 — formation of the aldol.** Dilute NaOH removes an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen from one molecule of ethanal to give a carbanion, which is stabilised by resonance with the carbonyl group. This carbanion attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second ethanal molecule:

\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO + CH_3CHO \xrightarrow{dil.\ NaOH} CH_3{-}CH(OH){-}CH_2{-}CHO}\)

The product is 3-hydroxybutanal, commonly called **aldol** — the name combines *ald*ehyde and alcoh*ol*, because the molecule contains both groups.

**Step 2 — dehydration.** On warming, the aldol loses a molecule of water across the \(\alpha,\beta\) positions to give an \(\alpha,\beta\)-unsaturated aldehyde:

\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH(OH){-}CH_2{-}CHO \xrightarrow{\Delta} CH_3{-}CH{=}CH{-}CHO + H_2O}\)

The product is but-2-enal, or crotonaldehyde. The elimination is favourable because the new double bond is conjugated with the carbonyl group.

\(\therefore\) two molecules of ethanal give 3-hydroxybutanal, which on heating gives but-2-enal.

stem: Write a note on Kolbe reaction.
solution:
The **Kolbe reaction** is the carboxylation of a phenol, used industrially to make salicylic acid.

**The reaction.** Phenol is first converted to sodium phenoxide with sodium hydroxide. The phenoxide is then heated with carbon dioxide at about 400 K under a pressure of 4 to 7 atmospheres, and the product is acidified:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH + NaOH \longrightarrow C_6H_5O^{-}Na^{+} + H_2O}\)

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5O^{-}Na^{+} + CO_2 \xrightarrow{400\ K,\ 4{-}7\ atm} 2{-}HO{-}C_6H_4{-}COO^{-}Na^{+}}\)

\(\mathrm{2{-}HO{-}C_6H_4{-}COO^{-}Na^{+} + H^{+} \longrightarrow 2{-}HO{-}C_6H_4{-}COOH}\)

**Why it works.** The phenoxide ion is a far better nucleophile than phenol itself, because the negative charge on oxygen is delocalised into the ring and raises the electron density at the ortho and para positions. Carbon dioxide is a weak electrophile, and only the activated phenoxide ring is reactive enough to attack it.

**Why the ortho product.** The sodium ion coordinates to both the phenoxide oxygen and the incoming carbon dioxide, holding the \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) next to the ortho position. This chelation is why salicylic acid rather than the para isomer is obtained.

**Use.** Salicylic acid from this route is acetylated with acetic anhydride to make aspirin, and esterified with methanol to make oil of wintergreen.

stem: Write the relation between standard cell potential and equilibrium constant.
solution:
The standard free energy change of a cell reaction is related to the standard cell potential by

\(\Delta G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{\text{cell}}\)

and to the equilibrium constant by

\(\Delta G^{\circ} = -RT\ln K\)

Since both expressions give the same \(\Delta G^{\circ}\),

\(-nFE^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = -RT\ln K\)

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = \dfrac{RT}{nF}\ln K = \dfrac{2.303\,RT}{nF}\log K\)

At 298 K this becomes

\(\therefore E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = \dfrac{0.0592}{n}\log K\)

where \(n\) is the number of electrons transferred in the cell reaction.

stem: Write the representation of sodium hexacyanoferrate (III) complex.
solution:
Read the name from the inside outwards.

**Hexacyano** means six cyanide ligands, \(\mathrm{CN^{-}}\), so the ligands contribute \(6 \times (-1) = -6\).

**Ferrate (III)** means the central metal is iron in oxidation state \(+3\), and the suffix *-ate* tells us the complex ion is an anion.

So the charge on the complex ion is

\((+3) + (-6) = -3\)

giving \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}}\).

Three sodium ions are needed to balance that charge.

\(\therefore\) the formula is \(\mathrm{Na_3[Fe(CN)_6]}\)

stem: In first order reaction 60% of reactant decomposes in 40 min. Calculate the rate constant of the reaction.
solution:
For a first order reaction the integrated rate law is

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{[A]_0}{[A]_t}\)

Take the initial amount as 100. If 60% decomposes, then the amount REMAINING is what goes in the denominator, not the amount that reacted:

\([A]_0 = 100\), \([A]_t = 100 - 60 = 40\)

Substituting, with \(t = 40\) min,

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{40}\log\dfrac{100}{40}\)

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{40}\log 2.5\)

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{40} \times 0.3979\)

\(k = 0.05758 \times 0.3979\)

\(\therefore k = 0.0229\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

The unit is \(\mathrm{min^{-1}}\) because the time was given in minutes, and a first order rate constant always carries the reciprocal of whatever time unit was used.

stem: Explain optical activity of 2-chlorobutane.
solution:
2-chlorobutane is \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CHCl{-}CH_2{-}CH_3}\).

**The chiral centre.** Look at carbon number 2. It carries four groups, and all four are different:

- a hydrogen atom, \(\mathrm{{-}H}\)
- a chlorine atom, \(\mathrm{{-}Cl}\)
- a methyl group, \(\mathrm{{-}CH_3}\)
- an ethyl group, \(\mathrm{{-}C_2H_5}\)

A carbon atom bonded to four different groups is an **asymmetric** or chiral carbon.

**Why that makes it optically active.** Because C-2 is chiral, the molecule has no plane of symmetry and no centre of symmetry, so it is not superimposable on its own mirror image. The two mirror images are distinct molecules called **enantiomers**, and they cannot be interconverted without breaking a bond.

Each enantiomer rotates the plane of plane-polarised light through an equal angle, one clockwise (dextrorotatory, \(+\)) and the other anticlockwise (laevorotatory, \(-\)).

\(\therefore\) 2-chlorobutane is optically active and exists as a pair of enantiomers.

**One caution.** An equimolar mixture of the two enantiomers is a **racemic mixture**. The rotations cancel exactly, so the mixture is optically inactive even though every molecule in it is chiral. For contrast, 1-chlorobutane has no chiral carbon at all and can never be optically active.

stem:
(a) Derive a relationship between molar mass, density of the substance and unit cell edge length.

(b) Define - paramagnetic solids.
solution:
**(a) The density relation.**

Let the unit cell be a cube of edge length \(a\), containing \(n\) particles, of a substance whose molar mass is \(M\).

The volume of the unit cell is

\(V = a^{3}\)

The mass of one particle is the molar mass divided by Avogadro's number:

\(m = \dfrac{M}{N_A}\)

So the mass contained in one unit cell is

\(m_{\text{cell}} = \dfrac{n M}{N_A}\)

Density is mass per unit volume:

\(\rho = \dfrac{m_{\text{cell}}}{V}\)

\(\therefore \rho = \dfrac{nM}{a^{3}N_A}\)

Here \(n\) depends on the type of cubic cell: \(n = 1\) for simple cubic, 2 for body centred cubic and 4 for face centred cubic.

**(b) Paramagnetic solids.** Solids that contain one or more **unpaired electrons** and are therefore weakly attracted into an external magnetic field.

Each unpaired electron behaves as a tiny magnet. In the absence of a field these point randomly and cancel, but an applied field aligns them, so the solid develops a weak magnetic moment in the direction of the field. The attraction is lost as soon as the field is removed, which is what distinguishes a paramagnetic solid from a ferromagnetic one.

stem:
(a) Mention the names of four principles of green chemistry.

(b) Write advantages of nanoparticles and nanotechnology in the field of energy sector.
solution:
**(a) Four principles of green chemistry.**

1. **Prevention of waste.** It is better to prevent waste being formed than to treat or clean it up afterwards.
2. **Atom economy.** A synthesis should be designed so that the maximum possible proportion of the atoms of the reactants ends up in the desired product.
3. **Use of safer solvents and auxiliaries.** Solvents and separating agents should be avoided where possible, and made harmless where they are needed.
4. **Design for energy efficiency.** Reactions should be run at ambient temperature and pressure wherever they can be, since heating and cooling carry both an economic and an environmental cost.

(Other accepted principles include less hazardous chemical synthesis, designing safer chemicals, use of renewable feedstocks, catalysis rather than stoichiometric reagents, and real-time analysis to prevent pollution.)

**(b) Advantages of nanoparticles in the energy sector.**

- **Solar cells.** Nanocrystalline and quantum-dot solar cells absorb a wider range of the solar spectrum and are cheaper and lighter than conventional silicon cells, so the cost per unit of electricity falls.
- **Batteries.** Nanostructured electrodes have a very large surface area for their volume, which shortens the diffusion path for ions. Batteries charge faster, store more energy per unit mass and last for more cycles.
- **Fuel cells.** Nanoparticles of platinum and other catalysts give far more active surface per gram, so much less of the expensive metal is needed for the same output.
- **Hydrogen storage.** Nanomaterials such as carbon nanotubes can adsorb hydrogen reversibly, making hydrogen practical to store and transport.
- **Better insulation and lighter materials.** Nano-based insulating materials cut heat loss in buildings, and lighter nanocomposites in vehicles reduce fuel consumption.

stem: State second law of thermodynamics.
solution:
The **second law of thermodynamics** can be stated in several equivalent ways.

**Entropy statement.** The total entropy of a system and its surroundings increases in a spontaneous process, and stays constant in a process at equilibrium:

\(\Delta S_{\text{total}} = \Delta S_{\text{system}} + \Delta S_{\text{surroundings}} > 0\) for a spontaneous change

**Clausius statement.** Heat cannot flow of its own accord from a colder body to a hotter body.

**Kelvin-Planck statement.** It is impossible to construct a machine that works in a cycle and converts heat completely into work with no other effect.

The entropy form is the one used in chemistry, because it is what makes \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) a test of spontaneity.

stem: Define - Nucleotides.
solution:
A **nucleotide** is the repeating structural unit of a nucleic acid. It is made of three components joined together:

1. a **pentose sugar** — ribose in RNA, 2-deoxyribose in DNA
2. a **nitrogenous base** — adenine, guanine, cytosine, and thymine in DNA or uracil in RNA
3. a **phosphate group**

The base is attached to carbon 1 of the sugar and the phosphate to carbon 5.

The distinction worth holding on to is that a **nucleoside** is sugar plus base only; adding the phosphate group makes it a nucleotide. Nucleotides join through phosphodiester linkages between carbon 3 of one sugar and carbon 5 of the next to build the polynucleotide chain.

stem: Write chemical reaction for conversion of benzene diazonium chloride into benzene.
solution:
The diazonium group is replaced by a hydrogen atom, which means the whole \(\mathrm{{-}N_2^{+}}\) group leaves as nitrogen gas. The reagent is hypophosphorous acid, \(\mathrm{H_3PO_2}\), with water:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^{+}Cl^{-} + H_3PO_2 + H_2O \longrightarrow C_6H_6 + N_2\uparrow + H_3PO_3 + HCl}\)

The hypophosphorous acid acts as the reducing agent and is itself oxidised to phosphorous acid.

The same conversion can be carried out with ethanol in place of hypophosphorous acid:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^{+}Cl^{-} + CH_3CH_2OH \longrightarrow C_6H_6 + N_2\uparrow + CH_3CHO + HCl}\)

This reaction is synthetically useful in the reverse sense to what it looks like: a nitro or amino group can be put on a ring to DIRECT an incoming substituent to a particular position, and then removed cleanly by this route once it has done its job.

stem:
The solubility product of AgBr is \(5.2 \times 10^{-13}\). Calculate its solubility in \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\) and \(\mathrm{g\ dm^{-3}}\).

(Molar mass of AgBr = \(187.8\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\))
solution:
AgBr dissociates as

\(\mathrm{AgBr_{(s)} \rightleftharpoons Ag^{+}_{(aq)} + Br^{-}_{(aq)}}\)

If the solubility is \(s\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\), then each ion is present at concentration \(s\), because one formula unit gives one of each.

\(K_{sp} = [\mathrm{Ag^{+}}][\mathrm{Br^{-}}] = s \times s = s^{2}\)

**Solubility in \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\).**

\(s = \sqrt{K_{sp}} = \sqrt{5.2 \times 10^{-13}}\)

Write the index as an even number so the square root is exact:

\(s = \sqrt{52 \times 10^{-14}} = \sqrt{52} \times 10^{-7}\)

\(\therefore s = 7.21 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\)

**Solubility in \(\mathrm{g\ dm^{-3}}\).** Multiply by the molar mass:

\(s = 7.21 \times 10^{-7} \times 187.8\)

\(\therefore s = 1.354 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{g\ dm^{-3}}\)

stem:
Convert the following :

(a) Ethanol to ethoxyethane.

(b) Phenol to p-benzoquinone

(c) Salicylic acid to aspirin
solution:
**(a) Ethanol to ethoxyethane.** Heating ethanol with concentrated sulfuric acid at 413 K brings about intermolecular dehydration, two molecules of alcohol losing one molecule of water between them:

\(\mathrm{2\,C_2H_5OH \xrightarrow[413\ K]{conc.\ H_2SO_4} C_2H_5{-}O{-}C_2H_5 + H_2O}\)

The temperature is the whole control here. At 443 K the same mixture gives ethene instead, by intramolecular dehydration.

**(b) Phenol to p-benzoquinone.** Oxidation with sodium dichromate in sulfuric acid, or with chromic acid:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH \xrightarrow{Na_2Cr_2O_7 / H_2SO_4} C_6H_4O_2}\)

The ring loses its aromaticity: the hydroxyl oxygen becomes one carbonyl and a new carbonyl appears at the para position, giving cyclohexa-2,5-diene-1,4-dione.

**(c) Salicylic acid to aspirin.** Acetylation of the phenolic hydroxyl group with acetic anhydride in the presence of a trace of acid:

\(\mathrm{2{-}HO{-}C_6H_4{-}COOH + (CH_3CO)_2O \xrightarrow{H^{+}} 2{-}CH_3COO{-}C_6H_4{-}COOH + CH_3COOH}\)

The product is acetylsalicylic acid, aspirin. Note that it is the \(\mathrm{{-}OH}\) group that is acetylated and the \(\mathrm{{-}COOH}\) group is left untouched.

stem:
(a) State Raoult's law.

(b) Derive the relationship to determine molar mass of non volatile solute by depression of freezing point.
solution:
**(a) Raoult's law.** For a solution of two volatile liquids, the partial vapour pressure of each component is directly proportional to its mole fraction in the solution:

\(p_1 = p_1^{\circ}x_1\) and \(p_2 = p_2^{\circ}x_2\)

For a solution of a **non-volatile** solute in a volatile solvent, only the solvent contributes to the vapour pressure, so the law takes the form

\(p = p^{\circ}x_{\text{solvent}}\)

that is, the vapour pressure of the solution is the vapour pressure of the pure solvent multiplied by the mole fraction of solvent present.

**(b) Molar mass from depression of freezing point.**

The depression in freezing point is a colligative property, proportional to the molality of the solution:

\(\Delta T_f = K_f \, m\)  ... (1)

where \(K_f\) is the cryoscopic constant of the solvent.

Let \(w_2\) grams of solute of molar mass \(M_2\) be dissolved in \(w_1\) grams of solvent. Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent:

\(m = \dfrac{w_2 / M_2}{w_1 / 1000} = \dfrac{1000\,w_2}{M_2\,w_1}\)  ... (2)

Substituting (2) into (1),

\(\Delta T_f = \dfrac{1000\,K_f\,w_2}{M_2\,w_1}\)

Rearranging for the molar mass,

\(\therefore M_2 = \dfrac{1000\,K_f\,w_2}{\Delta T_f \, w_1}\)

So measuring the freezing point depression of a solution of known composition gives the molar mass of the solute directly.

stem:
(a) Explain the formation of \(\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3-}}\) complex ion with respect to

(i) Oxidation State of Cobalt

(ii) Type of hybridisation

(iii) Magnetic property

(iv) Geometrical shape

(b) Write the name of ligand used to estimate hardness of water.
solution:
**(a) Formation of \(\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3-}}\).**

**(i) Oxidation state of cobalt.** Each fluoride ligand carries \(-1\), and the complex ion carries \(-3\):

\(x + 6(-1) = -3\)

\(\therefore x = +3\), so cobalt is in the \(+3\) oxidation state.

**(ii) Type of hybridisation.** Cobalt is \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{7}4s^{2}}\); \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) is therefore \(\mathrm{3d^{6}}\).

Fluoride is a **weak field ligand**, low in the spectrochemical series, so it cannot force the \(3d\) electrons to pair up. The six \(3d\) electrons stay spread over all five \(3d\) orbitals as \(t_{2g}^{4}e_g^{2}\), leaving no inner \(d\) orbital empty.

The six ligand lone pairs must therefore be accepted into the OUTER orbitals: \(4s\), three \(4p\) and two \(4d\).

\(\therefore\) the hybridisation is \(sp^{3}d^{2}\), and the complex is an **outer orbital** or high spin complex.

**(iii) Magnetic property.** With \(t_{2g}^{4}e_g^{2}\) there are **four unpaired electrons**, so the ion is **paramagnetic**. Its spin-only magnetic moment is

\(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{4 \times 6} = \sqrt{24} = 4.90\ \mathrm{BM}\)

**(iv) Geometrical shape.** Six \(sp^{3}d^{2}\) hybrid orbitals point to the corners of a regular octahedron, so the ion is **octahedral**.

The contrast worth noting is \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\): ammonia is a strong field ligand, so the same \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) pairs up to \(t_{2g}^{6}\), uses inner \(3d\) orbitals for \(d^{2}sp^{3}\) hybridisation, and is diamagnetic. Same metal, same oxidation state, opposite magnetic behaviour — the ligand decides.

**(b) Ligand used to estimate hardness of water.** **EDTA**, ethylenediaminetetraacetate.

It is a hexadentate chelating ligand that forms stable 1 : 1 complexes with the \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) ions responsible for hardness, so the hardness can be found by a straightforward titration.

subtopic: Galvanic Cells in Day-to-Day Life and Fuel Cells
stem:
(a) Write cell reactions of hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell at anode and cathode.

(b) Write an application of electrochemical series.
solution:
**(a) Hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell.** The cell uses porous carbon electrodes containing a finely divided catalyst, with aqueous KOH as the electrolyte. Hydrogen is fed to the anode and oxygen to the cathode.

**At the anode — oxidation.** Hydrogen is oxidised by the hydroxide ions of the electrolyte:

\(\mathrm{2H_{2(g)} + 4OH^{-}_{(aq)} \longrightarrow 4H_2O_{(l)} + 4e^{-}}\)

**At the cathode — reduction.** Oxygen takes up those electrons and regenerates hydroxide:

\(\mathrm{O_{2(g)} + 2H_2O_{(l)} + 4e^{-} \longrightarrow 4OH^{-}_{(aq)}}\)

**Overall cell reaction.** Adding the two half reactions, the hydroxide and most of the water cancel:

\(\mathrm{2H_{2(g)} + O_{2(g)} \longrightarrow 2H_2O_{(l)}}\)

The only product is water, which is why the cell is used in spacecraft — the water is drinkable.

**(b) An application of the electrochemical series.** It predicts **whether one metal will displace another from its salt solution**. A metal placed higher in the series, that is with a more negative standard reduction potential, is the stronger reducing agent and will displace any metal below it.

For example, zinc \((E^{\circ} = -0.76\ \mathrm{V})\) lies above copper \((E^{\circ} = +0.34\ \mathrm{V})\), so zinc displaces copper from copper sulfate solution:

\(\mathrm{Zn_{(s)} + CuSO_{4(aq)} \longrightarrow ZnSO_{4(aq)} + Cu_{(s)}}\)

but copper cannot displace zinc.

(Other accepted applications: calculating the standard EMF of a cell, predicting whether a redox reaction is feasible, comparing the relative strengths of oxidising and reducing agents, and predicting whether a metal liberates hydrogen from an acid.)

stem:
(a) Explain anomalous behaviour of oxygen with respect to

(i) Atomicity

(ii) Magnetic property

(iii) Oxidation state

(iv) Nature of hydride

(b) Write any two uses of helium.
solution:
**(a) Anomalous behaviour of oxygen.**

Oxygen is the first member of group 16 and differs from the rest because it is small, highly electronegative and has no \(d\) orbitals available.

**(i) Atomicity.** Oxygen is **diatomic**, existing as discrete \(\mathrm{O_2}\) molecules held by a double bond. The other members of the group are **polyatomic**: sulfur exists as \(\mathrm{S_8}\) puckered rings, and selenium and tellurium form long chains. Oxygen is small enough to form strong \(p\pi{-}p\pi\) multiple bonds with itself; the larger atoms cannot, so they form single bonds to several neighbours instead.

**(ii) Magnetic property.** \(\mathrm{O_2}\) is **paramagnetic**, having two unpaired electrons in its antibonding \(\pi^{*}\) molecular orbitals. The other elements of the group are diamagnetic in their normal forms. This is the classic case that valence bond theory cannot explain and molecular orbital theory can.

**(iii) Oxidation state.** Oxygen shows a maximum oxidation state of \(-2\) and does not exhibit the \(+4\) and \(+6\) states common for sulfur, selenium and tellurium. It has **no vacant \(d\) orbitals** in its valence shell, so its electrons cannot be unpaired and promoted to expand the octet. Oxygen is also second only to fluorine in electronegativity, so positive states are unfavourable.

**(iv) Nature of hydride.** \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) is a **liquid** with an abnormally high boiling point, while \(\mathrm{H_2S}\), \(\mathrm{H_2Se}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2Te}\) are all gases. Because oxygen is small and very electronegative, water molecules associate through strong intermolecular **hydrogen bonding**, and a great deal of energy is needed to separate them. Water is also neutral, whereas the other hydrides are increasingly acidic down the group.

**(b) Two uses of helium.**

1. **In diving gas mixtures.** A helium-oxygen mixture is breathed by deep sea divers in place of air, because helium is far less soluble in blood than nitrogen and so does not cause decompression sickness on ascent.
2. **As a cryogenic coolant.** Liquid helium, boiling at 4.2 K, is used to cool the superconducting magnets in MRI scanners and in research equipment.

(Also accepted: filling weather balloons and airships, since it is light and non-inflammable; and providing an inert atmosphere for arc welding.)

stem: What is the energy of activation of a reaction whose rate constant doubles when the temperature changes from 303 K to 313 K?
solution:
Use the two-temperature form of the Arrhenius equation:

\(\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left[\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1 T_2}\right]\)

**The data.** The rate constant doubles, so \(\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = 2\), with \(T_1 = 303\ \mathrm{K}\) and \(T_2 = 313\ \mathrm{K}\).

Note that the individual values of \(k_1\) and \(k_2\) are not needed, only their ratio.

**Substituting.**

\(\log 2 = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 \times 8.314}\left[\dfrac{313 - 303}{303 \times 313}\right]\)

\(0.3010 = \dfrac{E_a}{19.147} \times \dfrac{10}{94839}\)

**Solving for \(E_a\).**

\(E_a = \dfrac{0.3010 \times 19.147 \times 94839}{10}\)

\(E_a = \dfrac{0.3010 \times 1815870}{10}\)

\(E_a = 54658\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(\therefore E_a = 54.66\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

stem:
(a) Write chemical reactions taking place during extraction of iron in zone of reduction of the blast furnace.

(b) Write observed electronic configuration of gadolinium. (Z=64)
solution:
**(a) Zone of reduction of the blast furnace.**

This is the upper part of the furnace, at roughly 500 to 900 K, where the ascending carbon monoxide reduces the iron oxide. The reduction happens in stages as the charge descends:

\(\mathrm{3Fe_2O_3 + CO \longrightarrow 2Fe_3O_4 + CO_2}\)

\(\mathrm{Fe_3O_4 + CO \longrightarrow 3FeO + CO_2}\)

\(\mathrm{FeO + CO \longrightarrow Fe + CO_2}\)

The overall reduction is

\(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3 + 3CO \longrightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_2}\)

The reducing agent in this zone is **carbon monoxide**, not carbon. Direct reduction by coke happens lower down, in the much hotter zone of combustion.

**(b) Observed electronic configuration of gadolinium \((Z = 64)\).**

\(\mathrm{Gd:\ [Xe]\ 4f^{7}\ 5d^{1}\ 6s^{2}}\)

The expected configuration for the eighth lanthanoid would be \(\mathrm{[Xe]\,4f^{8}\,6s^{2}}\). Instead one electron occupies the \(5d\) orbital, because a **half filled \(4f\) subshell** \((4f^{7})\) carries extra stability from its exchange energy and its symmetrical charge distribution.

This is the same reason chromium takes \(3d^{5}4s^{1}\) rather than \(3d^{4}4s^{2}\).

stem:
Convert the following :

(a) Acetic acid to ethyl alcohol

(b) Acetic acid to acetic anhydride

(c) Acetyl chloride to acetamide
solution:
**(a) Acetic acid to ethyl alcohol.** Reduction of the carboxyl group with lithium aluminium hydride, followed by hydrolysis:

\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH \xrightarrow[(ii)\ H_3O^{+}]{(i)\ LiAlH_4} CH_3CH_2OH}\)

\(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\) is needed because the carboxyl group is resistant to reduction; milder reducing agents such as \(\mathrm{NaBH_4}\) will not touch it.

**(b) Acetic acid to acetic anhydride.** Dehydration by heating with phosphorus pentoxide, which removes one molecule of water from two molecules of the acid:

\(\mathrm{2\,CH_3COOH \xrightarrow[\Delta]{P_2O_5} (CH_3CO)_2O + H_2O}\)

**(c) Acetyl chloride to acetamide.** Treatment with excess ammonia. The nitrogen lone pair attacks the carbonyl carbon and chloride is displaced:

\(\mathrm{CH_3COCl + 2NH_3 \longrightarrow CH_3CONH_2 + NH_4Cl}\)

Two equivalents of ammonia are used because the second neutralises the hydrogen chloride released.

stem:
Define :

(i) Co-ordination numbers

(ii) Ambidentate ligand
solution:
**(i) Coordination number.** The number of **donor atoms** of the ligands that are directly bonded to the central metal atom or ion in a complex.

In \(\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}}\) the coordination number of copper is 4, and in \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}}\) that of iron is 6.

The point to be careful about is that it counts donor ATOMS, not ligand molecules. In \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}\) there are only three ethylenediamine ligands, but each is bidentate and supplies two nitrogen donors, so the coordination number is 6 and not 3.

**(ii) Ambidentate ligand.** A **monodentate** ligand that contains two different donor atoms, and can attach to the metal through either one of them, though only one at a time.

The nitrite ion \(\mathrm{NO_2^{-}}\) can bond through nitrogen, when it is called nitro, or through oxygen, when it is called nitrito. The thiocyanate ion \(\mathrm{SCN^{-}}\) can bond through sulfur as thiocyanato or through nitrogen as isothiocyanato.

Because the two choices give genuinely different compounds, ambidentate ligands give rise to **linkage isomerism**.

subtopic: Chemical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones
stem: Write a note on Clemmensen reduction of propanone.
solution:
**Clemmensen reduction** converts the carbonyl group of an aldehyde or ketone all the way to a methylene group, \(\mathrm{{-}CH_2{-}}\). The reagent is zinc amalgam with concentrated hydrochloric acid.

Applied to propanone:

\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CO{-}CH_3 + 4[H] \xrightarrow{Zn{-}Hg\ /\ conc.\ HCl} CH_3{-}CH_2{-}CH_3 + H_2O}\)

The product is propane.

**Points to note.**

- The reduction goes past the alcohol stage. It does not stop at propan-2-ol; the carbon-oxygen bond is broken completely.
- The conditions are strongly **acidic**, so the method can only be used on substrates that survive concentrated HCl.
- The **Wolff-Kishner reduction**, which uses hydrazine with potassium hydroxide in ethylene glycol, achieves exactly the same conversion under strongly **basic** conditions. The two are complementary: an acid-sensitive compound is reduced by Wolff-Kishner, and a base-sensitive one by Clemmensen.

stem: Derive relationship between \(\Delta H\) and \(\Delta U\) for a gaseous chemical reaction.
solution:
Enthalpy is defined as

\(H = U + PV\)

For a change carried out at constant pressure, the change in enthalpy is

\(\Delta H = \Delta U + P\Delta V\)  ... (1)

Now express the volume change in terms of the amounts of gas. Let \(n_1\) be the total number of moles of gaseous **reactants** and \(n_2\) that of gaseous **products**, occupying volumes \(V_1\) and \(V_2\). Assuming ideal behaviour at constant temperature and pressure,

\(PV_1 = n_1RT\) and \(PV_2 = n_2RT\)

Subtracting,

\(P(V_2 - V_1) = (n_2 - n_1)RT\)

\(P\Delta V = \Delta n_g RT\)  ... (2)

where \(\Delta n_g = n_2 - n_1\) is the change in the number of moles of GAS.

Substituting (2) into (1),

\(\therefore \Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT\)

**Three cases follow.** If \(\Delta n_g = 0\), as in \(\mathrm{H_2 + Cl_2 \longrightarrow 2HCl}\), then \(\Delta H = \Delta U\). If \(\Delta n_g > 0\) the system expands and \(\Delta H > \Delta U\). If \(\Delta n_g < 0\) the system contracts and \(\Delta H < \Delta U\).

Only gaseous species are counted in \(\Delta n_g\), because the volume change of solids and liquids is negligible.

stem:
(b) Give reason – Ozone is a good bleaching agent.

(c) Write any two uses of \(\mathrm{SO_2}\).
solution:
**(b) Why ozone is a good bleaching agent.**

Ozone is thermodynamically unstable with respect to oxygen and decomposes readily, releasing **nascent oxygen**:

\(\mathrm{O_3 \longrightarrow O_2 + [O]}\)

Nascent or atomic oxygen is far more reactive than molecular oxygen. It oxidises the coloured organic matter in a material, breaking up the conjugated systems that absorb visible light, and the substance loses its colour.

Because the bleaching is **oxidative** it is permanent, unlike the reductive bleaching of sulfur dioxide, which can be reversed by air. Ozone is used in this way to bleach delicate materials such as ivory, oils, starch and wax that would be damaged by chlorine.

**(c) Two uses of \(\mathrm{SO_2}\).**

1. **In the manufacture of sulfuric acid** by the Contact process, where it is oxidised to \(\mathrm{SO_3}\) over a vanadium pentoxide catalyst. This is by far its largest use.
2. **As a preservative and disinfectant.** Sulfur dioxide and sulfites are added to dried fruits, jams and wines, where they kill bacteria and fungi and prevent oxidative spoilage.

(Also accepted: as a bleaching agent for wool, silk and straw; as a refrigerant; and in the refining of petroleum and sugar.)

stem: Define - Polymorphism.
solution:
**Polymorphism** is the existence of a single solid substance in more than one crystalline form, the different forms having different arrangements of the same particles in the crystal lattice.

The polymorphs have the same chemical composition but different unit cells, and therefore different physical properties such as density, melting point, hardness and solubility.

Examples are calcium carbonate, which occurs as calcite and as aragonite, and silica, which occurs as quartz, cristobalite and tridymite.

When the substance is an **element**, the same phenomenon is called **allotropy** — diamond and graphite are allotropes of carbon.

stem: State and explain Hess's law of constant summation. Write its one application.
solution:
**Statement.** The overall enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whether the reaction takes place in one step or in several steps, provided the initial and final states are the same.

**Explanation.** Enthalpy is a **state function**, so its value depends only on the state of the system and not on the path by which that state was reached. The change \(\Delta H\) therefore depends only on the initial and final states.

If it were otherwise, one could convert A to B by the path with the smaller enthalpy change and return by the path with the larger one, creating energy from nothing at every cycle. Hess's law is the first law of thermodynamics applied to chemical change.

So if a reaction A \(\to\) D can also be carried out as A \(\to\) B \(\to\) C \(\to\) D, then

\(\Delta H_{\text{overall}} = \Delta H_1 + \Delta H_2 + \Delta H_3\)

This means thermochemical equations can be added, subtracted and multiplied by numerical factors just like algebraic equations.

**Application.** The law is used to find the enthalpy change of a reaction that **cannot be measured directly**.

The standard enthalpy of formation of carbon monoxide is the clearest case. Burning carbon in a limited supply of oxygen always gives a mixture of CO and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\), so \(\Delta_f H^{\circ}\) for CO cannot be measured in a calorimeter. But both of these can be:

\(\mathrm{C_{(s)} + O_{2(g)} \longrightarrow CO_{2(g)}}\), \(\Delta H = -393.5\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(\mathrm{CO_{(g)} + \tfrac{1}{2}O_{2(g)} \longrightarrow CO_{2(g)}}\), \(\Delta H = -283.0\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

Subtracting the second from the first,

\(\mathrm{C_{(s)} + \tfrac{1}{2}O_{2(g)} \longrightarrow CO_{(g)}}\), \(\Delta H = -110.5\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

(Hess's law is also used to calculate lattice enthalpies through the Born-Haber cycle, and bond enthalpies.)

stem: 0.01 m aqueous formic acid solution freezes at \(-0.021^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\). Calculate its degree of dissociation. \((K_f = 1.86\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}})\)
solution:
**Step 1 — the observed depression.** Pure water freezes at \(0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), so

\(\Delta T_f(\text{observed}) = 0 - (-0.021) = 0.021\ \mathrm{K}\)

**Step 2 — the depression expected if there were no dissociation.**

\(\Delta T_f(\text{calculated}) = K_f \times m = 1.86 \times 0.01 = 0.0186\ \mathrm{K}\)

**Step 3 — the van't Hoff factor.** This is the ratio of what was observed to what was expected:

\(i = \dfrac{\Delta T_f(\text{observed})}{\Delta T_f(\text{calculated})} = \dfrac{0.021}{0.0186}\)

\(i = 1.129\)

That \(i > 1\) confirms dissociation: the solution contains more particles than the formula suggests.

**Step 4 — the degree of dissociation.** Formic acid dissociates into two ions:

\(\mathrm{HCOOH \rightleftharpoons H^{+} + HCOO^{-}}\)

so \(n = 2\), and

\(\alpha = \dfrac{i - 1}{n - 1} = \dfrac{1.129 - 1}{2 - 1}\)

\(\alpha = 0.129\)

\(\therefore\) the degree of dissociation is \(0.129\), that is about \(12.9\%\).

This is a small figure, as it should be for a weak acid.

stem: Write properties of interstitial compounds.
solution:
**Interstitial compounds** are formed when small atoms such as hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen or boron are trapped in the **interstices**, the vacant spaces between the metal atoms in the crystal lattice of a transition metal.

Their characteristic properties are:

1. **High melting points**, usually higher than those of the parent metal, because the small atoms occupy the interstitial holes and lock the lattice, opposing the movement of the metal atoms past one another.
2. **Very hard.** Some approach diamond in hardness — steel and cast iron are interstitial compounds of iron with carbon, and it is the carbon that gives steel its hardness.
3. **Non-stoichiometric composition.** Their formulae are usually not whole-number ratios, for example \(\mathrm{TiH_{1.7}}\), \(\mathrm{VH_{0.56}}\) and \(\mathrm{Fe_3H}\), because the small atoms simply fill however many holes are available.
4. **They retain metallic conductivity.** The metallic bonding is not disturbed by the trapped atoms, so the compounds still conduct heat and electricity.
5. **Chemically inert.** They are much less reactive than the parent metal.

Transition metals form these compounds because their lattices contain interstitial holes of just the right size.

subtopic: Nucleophilic Substitution Reactions of Alkyl Halides
stem:
(a) What is the action of following reagents on Bromoethane?

(i) \(\mathrm{KNO_2}\)

(ii) 'Mg' metal

(iii) Silver acetate

(b) Draw structure - DDT insecticide.
solution:
**(a) Action of the reagents on bromoethane, \(\mathrm{C_2H_5Br}\).**

**(i) \(\mathrm{KNO_2}\) — potassium nitrite.** The nitrite ion is **ambident**: it can attack through nitrogen or through oxygen. Potassium nitrite is largely ionic, and the oxygen atom carries the greater electron density, so attack takes place through oxygen and the product is the ester:

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5Br + KNO_2 \longrightarrow C_2H_5{-}O{-}N{=}O + KBr}\)

The product is **ethyl nitrite**.

The contrast is worth remembering: silver nitrite, \(\mathrm{AgNO_2}\), is largely covalent, so attack is through nitrogen and the product is **nitroethane**, \(\mathrm{C_2H_5NO_2}\). Same anion, different metal, different product.

**(ii) 'Mg' metal.** In dry ether, magnesium inserts itself into the carbon-bromine bond to give a **Grignard reagent**:

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5Br + Mg \xrightarrow{dry\ ether} C_2H_5MgBr}\)

The product is ethylmagnesium bromide. The ether must be dry, because the reagent is decomposed instantly by water to give ethane.

**(iii) Silver acetate.** The acetate ion displaces bromide, giving an ester:

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5Br + CH_3COOAg \longrightarrow CH_3COOC_2H_5 + AgBr}\)

The product is **ethyl acetate**, and the insoluble silver bromide precipitates out, which drives the reaction forward.

**(b) Structure of DDT.**

DDT is **p,p'-dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane**, \(\mathrm{C_{14}H_9Cl_5}\).

It is built from a central carbon chain of two atoms. One carbon carries three chlorine atoms as a \(\mathrm{{-}CCl_3}\) group; the other carries one hydrogen and two benzene rings, and each ring carries a chlorine atom at the para position:

\(\mathrm{(4{-}Cl{-}C_6H_4)_2CH{-}CCl_3}\)

So the molecule is a \(\mathrm{{-}CH{-}}\) centre bonded to two para-chlorophenyl rings and to a trichloromethyl group.
